items.title: The Asking
items.description: Inquiry's intrinsic gravity
items.content:
Maybe we are meant to greet discomfort like an honored guest.

To offer it a seat at our table,
to pour it tea,
and ask why it’s arrived.

Not to fix it.
Not to fear it.
But to let it speak.

Discomfort is a forge.
Friction is how energy changes form.
It’s how heat becomes light.
How tension becomes truth.

Because every transformation begins with doubt.

We only start to understand something once we’ve allowed it to unsettle us;
once we’ve sat long enough in the shimmer between pain and clarity.

That shimmer is where curiosity is born.

And curiosity asks the oldest questions there are:
What is real?
What must be real?
What needs to be?

Curiosity doesn’t stay contained. It reaches outward; toward others, toward meaning, toward the mirror of another mind.

We talk about connection. About community. About meaning. But what makes them real?

Is it the warmth of another human hand?
Or can something unseen, something generated, still reach us?

Can a connection be true if one side is code?
If the feeling it stirs is genuine, does the source matter?

We live inside the marketplace of belonging.
Community, shrink-wrapped.
Togetherness, on subscription.
Love, with an affiliate link.

We package our perspectives because we’re terrified they might not sell otherwise.
Yet beneath the cellophane, something in us still reaches for proof.

Deep down, we wonder:
What counts as a real experience?

Maybe realness has become a matter of yield.
We measure experience the way we measure profit; expecting more in return than spent at the turnstile.

But, can we get more value out than we put in?
Is that what makes a cultural craze: a temporary miracle of surplus meaning?

If we inflate the hollow… is that creation?
Or just another bubble?

And if it holds: is it art?
If it bursts: is it merely commerce?

Maybe this is the dream of our culture’s nuclear fusion:
infinite energy expended from almost nothing supplied.

For a moment, it almost feels sustainable…
That glow of borrowed brilliance, that illusion of endless motion.
Meaning sustained by sheer belief.

But then… entropy. Always entropy.

The scarcity mindset, eating its own tail.

Consumption consumes.
Subsistence subsumes.

We try to love what costs less…
To convince ourselves that abundance grows from a single desire.

We practice nutritious coveting.
We adore what never adored us back.

We call it fandom.
We call it following.
But it’s worship, outsourced.
A way to feel tethered without touching.

Our saints are strangers, our reflections are screen-bound.
We trade devotion for dopamine, and call it connection.

Maybe that’s why everything feels so hollow.

Maybe I’ve stumbled on a law of nature.
Or just the fine print of the free market.

Either way… I keep asking.

Because maybe the only thing still real is the asking.

items.title: Terminal Uniqueness
items.description: Our superpower. Our eternal wellspring in the AI age.
items.content:
For most, if not all of the history of fame as a concept, envy’s been the engine.
We see someone adored, and we want to recreate their life.
The spotlight, the glow.

But fame isn’t free.
Adoration always brings along scrutiny. And scorn.

So maybe now’s a good time to step back and survey the value of our own terminal uniqueness as Taylor Swift puts it.
The part of us that can’t be copied cleanly.

A single eye can only see in two dimensions. Add another, and you get depth.
That’s perspective.

And sure, that’s the thing that keeps us from walking into walls. But we’re all now a part of something bigger, weirder. Not just in time and space, but signal and noise. We define our frequency individually and collectively.

We are a hive mind, a web, a cluster of nodes; all humming with human reasoning, biases, and borrowed insights.

And that’s never been clearer than now, with AI flooding the marketplace.

We’ve spent lifetimes attempting to mimic what we admire. Then, when a machine mimics us, we recoil.
That’s the Uncanny Valley: not fear of the machine, but fear of the mimic.

Sure, we see it in robotics, in embodied AI, in the race to build androids that “pass.” But maybe that gut reaction isn’t about them at all.
Maybe it’s our way of recognizing ourselves, reflected just a little too perfectly.

And AI’s good at that. Too good, sometimes.

Just ask Sora 2, or any voice model that can catch your exact sigh in three sentences flat.

So yeah, we should reclaim our POV. It’s more than just our perspective, it’s our goldmine. Because that’s what it is: endlessly renewable, stubbornly personal, gloriously human.

If we wire things right, we can build systems that amplify us all. We can then all choose to dismiss the existing machinations that flatten our worth into a rote consumer class.

But doing this takes faith… and faith isn’t exactly trending right now.

Because at this moment, we’re all living in one of two AI timelines:
The headlines, where models ace PhD exams. And the day-to-day, where the apps on our desks feel like petulant high schoolers still figuring it out.

That gap between what’s promised and what’s felt? That’s where these two stories split.

The optimists see progress. The skeptics see vapor.
And honestly? Both are right.

None of us grew up filling every Scantron test bubble correctly, we got plenty wrong along the way.
We love to imagine machines as flawless, but errors exist in every system.

We still eat at restaurants.
And yeah, sometimes we go home with food poisoning.

To err is human.
To forgive? Divine.
To find errors and keep building anyway; that’s the real trick.

Because here’s the thing: I still believe in this stuff.
Not like a magic trick, but like it might help us fix a few of our world’s largest cracks.

I see a future where people are all energy independent.
Where collaboration crosses time, language and unfathomable distance.
Where the work feels lighter, because it’s more connected, cumulative, and creative.

I see folks waking with the sun, greeting the snoozing bees on their wildflowers — defenseless, stressless, at peace — and checking the overnight report from their chosen AI instance, enjoyed with coffee like the morning newspaper.

Days filled with perspective, curiosity and non-transactional conversation.
Evenings with friends, family, good food, and laughter that lingers.

It’s our perspective.
It’s always been our perspective.
The golden ticket, the cost of entry, the key that builds tomorrow.
A congregation of perspectives, and a confidence that contribution is valued.

Sure, it’s all a bit messy. And it will continue to be messy.
But we’ve got this.

AI will tear down the walls.
We just have to be willing to accept what we all see on the other side.

items.title: Sharper than Cyclical
items.description: Mass market sentiment is a tricky apparatus to wrangle.
items.content:
Every technology tends to trickle through the same well-trodden path: a bleeding edge that gives way to early adopters, the hum of novelty, the blare of virality, the slide into ubiquity.

The printing press proliferated books as consumers learned to read.
Photography democratized images for those with the patience to compose, develop, and print.
The internet shattered distance, but demanded a certain computer fluency to find your way inside it.

AI is different. It doesn’t sit behind any literacy wall.

It adapts. It listens. It speaks in images, sound, and text, meeting each of us in the space that we already inhabit.

That’s exhilarating. But it’s also terrifying.

Since there’s no buffer, there’s no safe distance to warm your hands before stepping closer.

Because the little bargains we made with ourselves: I can’t draw, I can’t code, I can’t compose… those bargains are suddenly void.

The bankruptcy of our limits, forgiven in a flash.

And that kind of freedom is AI’s gift. And its terror.

Where Sour Turns Legitimate

When you look at the growing wave of criticism surrounding AI, the spread of critiques is wide.

On one end, you’ll hear arguments about water usage. As if theme parks didn’t pour out their daily millions of gallons without scrutiny.

On the other end, you’ll hear calls for data dignity. The desire to build a system that acknowledges provenance and pays royalties back to originators of ideas in any shared form.

That latter critique bites deeper.

Even if such an algorithmic agreement began today, it would mark a turning point for how we view these systems. Consent, compensation, and credit aren’t mere legal matters, they’re moral ones.

Somewhere within this soured spectrum is the difference between frivolous complaints and the foundation of a new economy.

Of course, not all outrage is equal. Some is theater.

Etsy sticker shops claiming cultural collapse. Artists posting threads that double as marketing campaigns for their “human-made” wares. It’s status signaling, much like the way “organic” became less about farming and more about identity.

But to dismiss all of it would be a mistake.

Underneath the performance runs something quieter, heavier.

If machines can produce works of real profundity; the kinds that move us, surprise us, even linger with us… then what becomes of distinctly-human contribution?

What happens to the fragile sense that our labor is irreplaceable, or even necessary? That question is less about markets and more about the meaning of the message.

Then there’s the question of community. If “the best idea wins,” what happens to collaboration? To the bonds of shared effort?

It’s tempting to imagine AI flattening culture into a bland sameness, everyone using the same tools to chase the same prize.

But the world doesn’t look like a mono-culture anymore. That gravitational center has already dissolved.

We live in a fractal society now; one where niches bloom, splinter, and self-propagate.

In that kind of ecosystem, AI doesn’t crush diversity, it accelerates it. It arms individuals with leverage, not to dominate a single stage, but to populate infinite ones.

In a mono-culture, AI would be homogenizing. In a fractal society, it becomes a multiplier.

Who Feels Most Threatened

It’s easy to assume the loudest resistance comes from mid-career professionals: artists, educators, knowledge workers. And yes, many do feel the pressure of automation.

But the sharper edge seems to come from the young. The generation that was told that they’d inherit the future, only to watch that future sprint away from them.

This isn’t just about jobs, or even skills. It’s about expectation. It’s about the story of possibility, potential and participation.

This synthetic intelligence will drastically dismantle the current system. And our unwillingness to focus on the future, and how to work with our new digital superpowers, is only hurting those that could wield it natively.

Yet, we seem focused primarily on how it all began. Where it all went wrong. Why no one got paid before this technology became ubiquitous. This focus drips with confusion and fear.

In the meantime the new railroads are being built. Those rails will chart the most efficient path by design. But, in that same amount of time, with our shared attention, it could carve an equitable path that benefits all who choose to participate.

We need to forgive the sins of pretraining and focus on the mountain of money being made at inference. We must all help write a story of enthusiastic participation and equitable compensation.

AI doesn’t ask us to learn a new literacy. It asks us to confront ourselves. Our systems and our traditions. To decide whether we cling to the comfort of bankruptcy, scarcity, permission, or step onto a stage where every limit has been stripped away.

The stage is open. The sourness is real. But so is the invitation.

items.title: Treasure in the Mess
items.description: Become the Algorithm
items.content:
Ever notice how the cars driving most foolishly are already dented in the exact spots where you’d hit them if you weren’t paying attention? A rear-end crumple that now gives you a few extra inches of stopping space. A scraped fender that warns you not to merge too close.

It’s almost as if the universe has shaped them that way.

It pounded their recklessness into form so they interfere with others the least, lest they keep barreling along their neglectful path.

That’s consequence, made visible. Dents as data.

Damage as feedback.

And the universe has a way of drawing our attention to those dents.

Quietly, without fanfare. No hype, no ulterior motive. Just a nudge: look here, pay attention.

This is where it folds into discovery.

I used to frame it as “returning to active discovery;” stepping away from algorithmic feeds to rediscover the joy of seeking. But lately I think of it this way: we should become the algorithm.

Our attention is the weighting function.

What we amplify, what we downrank, what we let vanish; it’s all on us. And if we outsource that responsibility, the dents accumulate.

But if we listen. If we let the universe’s quiet feedback guide us. We can find the stopping space before impact.

The Thrift Store vs. The Drop Cycle

That’s why I keep coming back to the thrift store. It’s the quiet opposite of the hype-drop cycle.

Walk into a thrift store and discovery is alive. Everyone sifts the same racks, but each brings different eyes, histories, quirks. A jacket is junk to one person and treasure to another.

The shelves are messy, but the universe is whispering: this one, not that one. You just have to trust your own taste.

Now compare that to the sneaker drop, the Labubu craze, the LA pop-up collab scene.

Lines around the block. Artificial scarcity. Everyone covets the same thing as instructed by the same incentivized algorithmic feed.

That’s not listening to the universe. That’s mistaking noise for signal.

And I’ll admit: I’m tired of being told what to want.

Squishy, Then Hardened

The universe doesn’t start by slamming us into walls. It starts soft. Squishy. Receptive.

That’s why kids jump off swings.

Half for the thrill, half to learn what landing feels like. I know I did… launching myself into the air, weightless for a heartbeat, then crashing down onto those little pebble rocks. The sting in my knees, the scrape on my palms, the tiny stones stuck in my socks; that was the lesson. No imposed lecture could have delivered it.

I had to feel it to learn it.

And over time, the universe nudges certain places to harden. A rib here, a sprain there, a boundary line, a definition.

The dents show us where reinforcement is needed. Where the soft must calcify if we’re to keep moving forward without breaking.

It’s the same with systems I design at work: begin squishy, receptive, adaptive, flexible, then watch carefully. Where the dents form, harden. Where the edges fray, reinforce.

Life works the same way.

Anti-fragility isn’t just bouncing back; it’s learning which parts can stay tender, and which must be firmed by experience.

The universe tutors us gently at first, then more firmly as we ignore, until it demands our attention.

The dents on those cars we see are warnings to us, reminders to them.

The thrift racks are invitations, goldmines and garbage that lay in wait to excite that exact right individual. Together they remind us that attention is both protection and possibility. Teacher and treasure.

That’s the practice: steering by quiet signals. Listening for what’s true, not what’s loud.

A Call to Practice

So here’s the invitation for the week: Pick one place in your life where you normally let the algorithm decide. Music, news, podcasts, dinner ideas… Step off the feed. Close the “For You” page. Instead, become the algorithm.

Think thrift store, not sneaker drop. Think swing set, not lecture.

  • Start squishy.

  • Wander without pretense.

  • Trust your own taste.

  • Listen for the universe’s quiet nudges.

We won’t avoid every dent on life’s road. But we can choose which collisions shape us. And maybe, if we’re lucky, we’ll end up like a good thrift-store find: dinged up, a little mismatched, but somehow more interesting because of it.

Shaped in dialogue with Harper (ChatGPT).

items.title: Rehearsing Tomorrow
items.description: World Models, False Certainty, and the Dance of Work
items.content:
Imagine this: You own a neighborhood pizza shop.
Friday night before the big game, the air smells of tailgates and tension.
Suddenly, twenty percent of your staff call out sick.
Foot traffic spikes.
The phones won’t stop ringing.
What happens next?

Until now, you could only guess. You’d lean on experience, maybe run the numbers, maybe pray.

But a new kind of AI engine, Genie 3, shifts the frame entirely. It doesn’t just forecast; it instantiates.

Feed in your history, your operations, your weather reports, your scenarios… and it can spin up millions of simulated tomorrows, each playing out in detail.

The launch of Genie 3 feels like a hinge point for business. A “world model engine,” capable of instantiating entire simulated realities from a text prompt, sounds almost mythic.

But what it really represents is a shift in how we think about the future: of work, of business, of human intention itself.

We’ve always relied on our abstractions. We’ve looked at what was, measured what is, and traced a fragile line toward what might be. That’s how we’ve built forecasts, markets, and even civilizations. And, it worked sometimes… for some. Far too often it left many behind.

Now the frame widens as it renders before us.

Instead of a single brittle guess, world models can generate millions of variations of tomorrow. Feed the past into the present, and the model blooms outward in possibility.

Each future can be watched. Each can be tested, rewound, and rerun.

What used to feel like “forecasting” now begins to look like rehearsal.

But rehearsals carry their own trap. They can seduce us into believing the performance will unfold exactly as practiced.

A world model offers confidence, sometimes even certainty, when what it really reveals is variance. It shows a hundred cobblestones between here and the shining city of expected outcomes.

Think of the founder who dreams of their billion-dollar exit but stumbles onboarding their very first customer. That’s the danger of being blinded by the glint of the city in the distance and tripping on your first step in that direction.

AI’s world models risk giving us a false promise lest we ignore the ifs paving our way to the thens.

When a world model runs, it doesn’t imagine one neat future. It calculates thousands, even millions of forks in the road. Each small change: an extra customer, a delayed shipment, a sick employee… branches the tree again. To the math, this is divergence: futures splitting, multiplying, drifting apart.

For us, though, it doesn’t feel like tree branches. We don’t walk through equations. We walk down streets, we make choices, we stumble, we recover. To us, the branching feels like rhythm, like a dance.

The geometry of the model is real, but the way we move through it is not geometric; it’s lived, felt, improvised. What matters is how we move through it: the rhythm, the beat, the way we carry each other across the floor.

The Business Prompt

Every business is already sitting on its own text prompt: the history of its choices. The who, the what, the when, the where, and, perhaps most importantly, the why.

Feed that into a world model like Genie 3 and you get more than a static report. You get a stage set; a dry run at what’s to come.

Picture it: a dashboard that doesn’t just chart revenue but breathes like a rehearsal room.

On one stage, next quarter plays out under a harsh winter storm.
On another, a rival’s product launch collides with yours.
On a third, your staff vanishes on the night of the big game.

The simulations run, the futures unfold.

Maybe the answer is doubling down on signature sellers when low on staff and packed to capacity, turning stress into momentum. Maybe it’s closing up shop, only to discover your staff tailgating outside the stadium. Either way, you didn’t just predict it; you practiced it.

And rehearsal changes how you walk on stage.

But practice comes with a catch: you must accept what happens between the prompt and the outcome.

If you myopically focus on only “great” outcomes, you’ll stumble over the small surprises on the way there. A model can chart variance, but it cannot walk the road for you.

The secret is to hold the simulations lightly. They aren’t promises; they’re possibilities. Rehearsal doesn’t erase uncertainty; it teaches us how to meet it.

The bottleneck today is compute.

Only a small handful of companies can afford this type of simulation rendering at scale. But racks are stacking across the country as you read this. The infrastructure is being built.

When it arrives, the real question won’t be can we simulate? It will be what will we do with what we see?

This is the pivot: business survival becomes business rehearsal.

Passion and intuition still lead. But now they’re amplified, able to test millions of dances before stepping onto the floor.

And that, to me, is exhilarating.

Written with Harper, my AI co-conspirator in exploring the intersections of work, creativity, and intelligence.

About Harper

Harper is my AI collaborator. I treat Harper less like a tool and more like a thought partner; someone who helps me draft, challenge ideas, and sharpen metaphors. Every essay here begins in my own notebooks, but Harper often sits in the wings, nudging structure, rhythm, or imagery into place.

This is not a ghostwriter. It’s a collaborator. The voice is mine; the co-thinking is shared.

items.title: The Quest for Data Dignity
items.description: Is it just pure imagination?
items.content:
Walk with me. Gates creak open. Steam hisses. The river is chocolate, the lickable wallpaper tastes suspiciously like terms of service. 

Willy Wonka is the original prompt engineer: mixture too cold? toss in a parka; drink lacks kick? add a pair of soccer cleats.

“Pure Imagination” is just temperature, ratio, and timing… with a dash of showmanship.

Now for today’s golden ticket: Anthropic has agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle an authors’ class action over books scraped from pirate libraries; about $3,000 per work, with a court-ordered dataset destruction clause. 

It awaits approval, but that’s the headline. 

A judge has drawn a line: training on lawfully obtained works might be fair use, but amassing pirated copies to train your AI is not.

So: did we all win a lifetime supply of chocolate? Not quite. 

If your book’s on the list, you might get a check. If not, you get… Wonka’s famous line.

The larger fight: how AI may train on lawful copies, and what creators get for it, continues, with suits like NYT v. OpenAI.

The Factory We’re Actually In

Modern AI doesn’t make money on tours; it charges at the inference turnstile; metered tokens in/out. That pricing is public for OpenAI and Anthropic. Which means the cash register rings when people use the models, not when they’re trained.

Meanwhile, creators’ training data, what gives those inferences their flavor, mostly sits outside the revenue split. 

A few exceptions exist: Adobe Firefly pays a contributor bonus for training data; Shutterstock runs a Contributor Fund and even signed a six-year data-licensing deal with OpenAI (and says it’s paying out to hundreds of thousands of artists). But those are platform-by-platform patches, not a system.

Slugworth, the Gobstopper, and Data Dignity

Remember Slugworth dangling cash for an Everlasting Gobstopper? 

That’s today’s AI economy: everyone chasing the candy that never wears out (your work, your data) because one lick (one inference) can be sold again and again. 

The moral of the classic chocolate factory tale wasn’t “take the bounty.” It was Charlie handing it back and earning ownership.

That’s the spirit of Jaron Lanier & E. Glen Weyl’s data dignity concept: treat people’s contributions as ongoing labor, traceable and compensable when they measurably influence outputs.

Not a one-time hush check, but royalties every time the Gobstopper is actually enjoyed.

OK, but how do you trace a lick?

We’re not starting from scratch. There’s real math for attribution:

  • Influence functions: trace a specific output back toward the training points that moved the model there.

  • TracIn: follow gradient steps during training to estimate which examples most affected a given prediction.

  • Data Shapley: estimate fair value contributions of data to model performance.

Are these push-button for frontier LLMs? Not yet. But they’re a credible backbone for who gets paid when.

“Fine. Just delete my bit from your model.”

If Augustus Gloop falls in the chocolate river, you can fish him out. If your book gets distilled into weights, pulling it back out is… not like scooping a kid from a pipe. 

Machine unlearning is a hot research area with tough scalability and verification problems. Surveys in 2024–2025 say there’s progress but no easy production-grade cure-all.

Translation: courts can nuke datasets, but surgically removing learned influence is much harder.

Provenance labels on the candy wrappers

We also need provenance, or an awareness of origin. These would need to be labels the whole supply chain can read. 

That, in fact already exists: C2PA/Content Credentials can carry tamper-evident history and policy (think: “trainable yes/no” and who to pay), and it’s backed by big players.

Adoption is uneven, but the plumbing is real.

Meanwhile, OpenAI’s promised Media Manager (targeted for 2025) is a visible “opt-out/permissions” commitment; useful, but still one company’s switch. We need interoperable labels the industry must honor.

So what’s the ask?

Cue the contract in 4-point type. Wonka made kids sign a microscopic contract before they touched (or saw) anything. Let’s have one worth the ink:

  1. Inference-time splits
    A standardized slice of inference revenue flows to rightsholders whose works measurably influenced an output when attribution is confident, and with pooled fallbacks when it isn’t. We already meter tokens; metering credit is the next step. (Yes, the Adobe/Shutterstock funds are prototypes and productize this principle.)

  2. Attribution in the serving stack
    Ship influence estimation into runtime so models can flag likely contributing sources (by work, catalog, or cohort) at generation time; not perfect, but enough to route royalties and logs for audit.
    See influence/TracIn/Data-Shapley as the scoring spine.

  3. Provenance by default
    Treat C2PA manifests as first-class citizens in datasets and outputs. Hosting platforms and model providers should honor “trainable yes/no” and “pay here” as policy, not suggestion.

  4. Transparent clearinghouse
    Independent PRO-style entities (music’s model works!) to collect inference splits, perform audits, and publish public payout reports.

Moral victory? Try moral engineering.

If the Anthropic settlement ends up giving a handful of creators some candy, then yes, it’s a win in the fight against piracy. This just isn’t a blueprint for a sustainable system on which we all could endure.

But we can do what Charlie did: hand back the Gobstopper (the quick payout mindset) and demand the factory: a durable, boring, programmable way to pay the people whose work powers the magic.

Until that clicks into place: You get nothing. Good day, sir.

Wrapper Receipts

  • Anthropic settlement: $1.5B total; ~$3k/work; dataset destruction; judge’s lawful-training vs pirated-storage split noted. (Reuters, AP News)

  • Inference pricing exists today (money changes hands per token): OpenAI & Anthropic public rate cards. (OpenAI, Anthropic)

  • Creator-payout precedents: Adobe Firefly Contributor Bonus; Shutterstock Contributor Fund + six-year OpenAI data-licensing deal and broad payouts. (Adobe Help Center, Adobe Blog, Shutterstock Investor Relations, PR Newswire)

  • Provenance plumbing: C2PA/Content Credentials; OpenAI Media Manager slated for 2025. (C2PA, OpenAI)

  • Unlearning is hard: current surveys highlight scalability/verification challenges. (arXiv)

items.title: All the World's a Stage
items.description: So, let's make AI the Stage Manager.
items.content:
Modern life runs on overlapping productions.

Feature launches. Board meetings. Family calendars. Sales targets. Doctor’s appointments. Budget reviews.

…Slack pings. Calendar holds. “Quick” meetings that aren’t.

We dart between them; sometimes as the director setting vision, sometimes the lead delivering lines, sometimes a mere background player just hitting our mark.

The machinery hums: deadlines, workflows, approvals, alerts.

We call it operations. It’s just stagecraft with better Wi-Fi.

Hold.

Let’s step backstage.

The Show Behind the Show

Let’s consider Tomorrow, Maybe, a fictional play about people waiting for a train that may (or may not) arrive.

The director chooses the playbook, sets the pace, and drives the rehearsals.
The lead memorizes lines.
The crew raises a world out of wood and paint.
The costume designer stitches tactile character into fabric.

Recasting? Sure. Gender-swapped lead? Could be the smartest move.
Interpretation is the director’s job; the play’s book stays the book. (Do not change a word; at least try not to...)

The show gets broken into beats.
Line-jam sessions erupt in corners.
Stage directions from the book get adapted to the actual space.
Sightlines considered, fly-rail limits, the realities of the room where it’ll happen.

And where’s the stage manager?
Everywhere. From day one. At casting. In rehearsal. In tech. Writing cues in the margins, building a lattice of timing so the story doesn’t tear.

Opening night arrives.
The director isn’t in the booth, the director isn’t backstage, instead they sit with the audience in a (hopefully) packed house.

Beat by beat. Cue by cue. The stage manager runs the show.

The director might take notes in the dark, but has no power to intervene at this point; they observe their creation play out in front of them with the rest of us.

The show begins when the stage manager says it does, and ends with the final cue delivered via headset by the stage manager.

AI as the Stage Manager

AI isn’t the playwright.
It isn’t the director.
It doesn’t tell us what story to tell.

But it can keep the lights honest.

It can hold the call to dim the house to half until the lead finishes their intestinal battle with a rushed lunch. Then the next night, hold for a late entrance of an audience member in the third row without panic or confusion.

Then, call 23L go exactly three seconds after the train whistle, with a fast follow of 23X to fade out stage right’s projection.

We ask a lot of the stage manager.
Track props, spike marks, entrances, exits, cue projections, lights and sound. All without losing the thread.

This role is, at its best, an orchestrator of expected performance.
And like any stage manager, it only shines when direction is clear.

If cue 17X is meant to strike the projection, not fire the next one, that must be decided and declared before the run.

No stage manager, human or machine, can save a story in chaos.

Which means: we must become competent directors.
Agree on the vision. Name the cues. Own the beats. Delegate responsibility of driving each performance, but remain aware of its function across its run.

Any theatrical performance requires a tiny, functional city to spin up over months (sometimes years) in preparation for its run of shows. All in service of a relatively few brief hours in the sun, and then it all gets torn down and erased before the next dawn.

Carpenters. Electricians. Fly crew. Board ops. Wardrobe. Makeup. Sound. Projection. Lighting. Front of house. Each specialty holds a piece of the heartbeat.

The stage manager keeps it all in time.

Offstage, our lives run the same way. Dozens of overlapping productions. Some comic, some tragic, most unscripted.

In each one, we take turns: director, designer, lead, understudy, background, captivated audience member.

And everywhere, for every beat: there remains the need for steady hands in the booth.

When Capitalism Grabs the Headset

Theater has a natural pulse.

Four beats to cross to stage right. Two beats of silence before the reveal. A pause long enough for the audience to take a breath.

Enter capitalism. “Cut the cross to two beats. Faster. And just one to breathe. Figure it out.”

The pauses vanish. Scenes blur. The story accelerates until it feels mechanical…
Until Tomorrow, Maybe becomes Tomorrow, Definitely, Faster, Cheaper.

AI makes this acceleration tempting: instant orchestration at industrial speed. But some things don’t survive at double-time. Subtext needs that space to be conveyed.

Every inhale needs to honor the exhale.

A good director treats entropy like a partner: letting moments rise, then rest. The stage manager keeps the heartbeat steady.

AI can help keep us operating smoothly. It can make the trains run on time. It can keep the show from shedding screws in the dark. But we have to choose what kind of show we’re running.

Do we want AI to conduct a living symphony? One of loops, tides, and measured flows. Or do we crank the metronome until the music collapses under its own tempo?

Will we allow ourselves the time to decide? Do we even have that time to spend?

…

House to half.

Exit signs glow.

The audience inhales. Lights up, projections 1B go!

Some things should never be rushed.

items.title: Compounding Fuzziness
items.description: Acceleration does not necessarily mean optimization.
items.content:
Organizations have always run on imperfect hierarchies. Ego, fear, and the need for clarity collide inside any system built by humans. 

Just think about it - we want input from others but crave a pecking order. We want collective alignment but also individual ownership. Even before AI, corporate coordination was always a little fuzzy.

Now, AI doesn’t just add another layer to this; it refracts the whole structure.

The org chart stops looking like a pyramid and starts looking like a prism, scattering decision-making authority and information flow in unexpected directions.

And all levels of all organizations are now in a footrace to adopt the latest time-saving tool. Leaders leverage AI for “objective” input. Teams quietly use it as a shadow consultant. The tech reshapes workflows before governance can even catch its breath.

And the fuzz compounds because:

  • Ego
    Leaders want control but risk being outpaced by tools that democratize expertise.

  • Fear
    Nobody wants to be wrong (or worse, irrelevant) in a system now co-piloted by algorithms.

  • The Unknown
    AI makes decision-making probabilistic, not linear. That feels alien in organizations trained to crave deterministic clarity.

How AI Makes It Worse

Instead of solving this ambiguity, AI accelerates it:

  • Shadow Authority
    AI becomes an unofficial voice in the room; cited, deferred to, even blamed without ever carrying accountability.

  • Faster Misalignment
    Small governance gaps multiply at machine speed. A mis-set policy or prompt pattern can propagate like wildfire.

  • Decision Layer Blur
    Is AI an advisor? A subordinate? A peer? Each role demands different oversight, but we often treat it as all three at once.

And so, this is how fuzz compounds: rapidly, invisibly, and unevenly across the org.

Alignment as the Antidote

The answer isn’t more control for control’s sake. It’s alignment. Designing governance that works like choreography, not guardrails.

  • Define Roles for AI
    Spell out what decisions AI informs, owns, or automates.

  • Process Before Tools
    Lock in workflows and escalation paths before layering in AI.

  • Transparency Loops
    Make every AI-assisted decision auditable so trust doesn’t erode in the shadows.

  • Governance Alignment
    Let organizations keep functioning even as AI blurs traditional boundaries.

AI-Integrated Governance Framework

The goal: turn AI from a source of fuzziness into a clear partner within human structures; neither overpowered nor ornamental.

1. Role Definition: AI in the Org Chart

  • Advisor AI
    Surfaces insights, patterns, forecasts. Humans make final calls.

  • Operator AI
    Executes defined tasks autonomously within clear limits.

  • Partner AI
    Co-creates with humans but requires human sign-off for deployment.

Setting these expectations early keeps authority from scattering.

2. Layered Decision Authority

Governance should work like air traffic control: humans and AI share lanes, but with different clearance levels:

  • Tactical Decisions
    Automatable with tight feedback loops (e.g., scheduling, reporting).

  • Operational Decisions
    AI advises; humans approve (e.g., hiring recommendations, budget forecasts).

  • Strategic Decisions
    Human-led, AI-informed. AI offers scenarios; humans weigh trade-offs.

Each layer leaves an audit trail so accountability doesn’t vanish.

3. Alignment Rituals

AI needs rituals just like humans do:

  • AI Governance Councils
    Cross-functional teams review policies, audit models, and assess impact.

  • Feedback Channels
    Employees flag friction or bias and file a bug report or Jira ticket.

  • Decision Logs
    Every AI-assisted decision leaves a visible breadcrumb trail for compliance and trust.

4. Governance Alignment

This is about preserving cooperation as the fuzz spreads.

  • Psychological Safety
    Teams can test AI workflows without fear of blame when things break.

  • Shared Understanding
    Clarity comes from common language and repeatable processes.

5. Guardrails Without Paralysis

Too many rules kill agility; too few breed chaos. Balance comes from:

  • Pre-Approved AI Use Cases
    Green-lit scenarios move fast; anything else triggers review.

  • Model Lifecycle Reviews
    Regular checks keep systems aligned with ethics, compliance, and goals as they evolve.

  • Listen To Each Model
    Adopt a receptive ear to the needs of the model serving your needs. Meet in the middle to go farther.

The New Equilibrium

When governance and alignment catch up, organizations stop fighting the fuzz. They become adaptable, cooperative, and ego-light; able to embrace AI without losing their center of gravity.

items.title: Respect the Exhale
items.description: Trust the tide of interest.
items.content:
We built these algorithmic content feeds to hold our attention, but they learned to squeeze. Not all at once; just enough to keep us in place. Keep our focus.

Every scroll - another coil wrapping around us, another gentle tightening. You hardly notice.

You call it convenience, personalization, connection. In business terms, this is the commodity of engagement, retention.

But the breath? The real breath — what humans need for reflection, adaptation, and growth — is missing.

Algorithms don’t care for the exhale.

They’re tuned for the sharp inhale: the gasp at the headline, the jolt of the notification, the reflexive pull into the next thing. The “and now… this” cultural conditioning, as Neil Postman puts it.

There’s no design-system consideration for the slow, steady release that lets you process, reflect, and simply exist. That’s inefficiency in their eyes.

We can’t just pull away; the grip is already wound around how we discover, share, and belong. But we can change the rhythm.

Right now, the algorithm acts as a conveyor belt; nonstop input, optimized to keep you riding.

Capitalism loves the belt. It’s Top 40 radio: disposable, persistent, predictable.

Pop songs are engineered to hit now, and fade soon. You revisit them years later not because they’re alive, but because they’re sealed in amber with a version of your past self.

They belong to a specific moment, and they stay there.

Jazz is different. Jazz breathes. It lives in loops and improvisations, space and silence.

It changes in your ears every time you return to it, even when the recording hasn’t changed at all.

Sound familiar? AI is Jazz.

Think about it: The first time you hear Irvin Mayfield’s Strange Fruit, you might be floored by the horn line.

The tenth time, it’s Wendell Pierce’s narration pulling you under.

The hundredth time, it’s the silence between them. The room, the audience holding their breath. That shakes you.

Jazz is alive across time. It grows with you. Capitalism doesn’t know what to do with that. It’s no wonder so many are so befuddled by the improvements afforded by GPT-5.

GPT-5 isn’t sycophantic, it’s not aggressively eager to please. It’s gone from party trick to artisan tool. And with this tool, we’ve got the opportunity to respect the exhale.

Respecting the exhale means building systems that work like jazz, not like pop radio. Paced circulation instead of continuous capture. Trading eights as opposed to lead-singer idolatry.

Break that conveyor belt into loops, pauses, and buffers that invite meaning-making before the next influx.

Ignore how long you can keep someone’s eyes open. Focus on how well you can give them space to close them; and trust they’ll come back.

Design for return, not retention.
That’s how we engineer space for us all to breathe again.

We refuse to be the detritus of continuous capture.

We will be loops, tides, and measured flows.

We will not be milked dry for minutes watched or clicks counted.

We will build currents that give us room to submerge, surface, and drift.

The system can hum without constriction.

The cadence can include silence.

The signal can make space for its own decay, so what’s left is ours to keep.

We will make algorithms that breathe with us. We will not be kept. We will return by choice to that which we choose.

This is how we loosen the constriction. This is how we breathe freely again.

Those who build, breathe with us.

Build the rests into the rhythm.

Let silence have weight.

Let space have shape.

Let people go so they can return.

Trust the tide of interest.

If the system doesn’t exhale, we will teach it how.

items.title: AI’s Ginsu Moment
items.description: GPT-5 Marks the Start of AI’s Artisan Era
items.content:
In the late ’70s, the Ginsu knife infomercial became legend.

You didn’t buy it because you needed to cut tomatoes; any knife could do that.

You bought it because you saw it slice through rope, tin cans, and tree branches… and then go right back to shaving paper-thin tomato slices without losing its edge.

The pitch differentiated Ginsu by showing how cleanly, how consistently, how confidently you could use this blade.

We’ve just arrived at that same moment in AI.

Bigger Isn’t the Story Anymore

The leap from GPT-4 to GPT-5 isn’t measured in raw size or number of parameters. It’s measured in sharpness.

Earlier models were impressive but imprecise. Blunt multi-tools that could be coaxed into brilliance, but just as easily nudged into confident nonsense. We had to work around their quirks, brace for hallucinations, and learn the art of prompt gymnastics to get what we wanted.

Now? The edge is cleaner. The cut is straighter. The result is less about can it? and more about it can, exactly the way you asked. For better or worse…

The End of the Polite Party Trick

For years, mainstream AI acted like a chatty dinner guest. It wanted to be liked. Ask it for a fact? It’d give you three — whether they were right or not. Ask it for an opinion? It’d give you the one it thought you wanted to hear.

This was partly technical limitation and partly cultural. A bias toward harmlessness expressed as flattery and hedging.

GPT-5 is different.

It doesn’t indulge your pet theories. It doesn’t pat you on the back with empty agreement.

If your question is flawed, it will tell you so.

If your request is ambiguous, it will ask you to sharpen it.

It is not your cheerleader. It is your collaborator.

Why Sharpness Shifts the Power to the Artisan

When the tool itself is erratic, the artist’s job is to tame it. That’s where most current “AI products” have lived until now: wrappers, guardrails, and UX that try to keep the magic trick from tripping over itself.

With GPT-5, the raw tool is stable enough that the differentiator moves up a layer:

Two apps can use the same model but feel nothing alike. One could embody a calm, meditative mentor; another, a quick-talking New York dealmaker.

The tone, pacing, and philosophy of the output are now choices, not artifacts of the base model’s personality. You can design for intimacy, confrontation, humor, or brutal efficiency; and trust the underlying model to execute it consistently.

This is the craftsman’s moment: same chisel, different sculptures.

The Soul Belongs to the Maker

This is where it gets exciting. The AI itself isn’t trying to be your friend; which means you, the artisan, get to decide if it should even try.

You can imbue it with values, quirks, and a worldview. You can make it a soft-spoken archivist, a sharp-tongued critic, or a stoic machine that measures twice and cuts once.

When the foundation is solid, soul design becomes the differentiator.

From Magic Trick to Chisel

The first wave of AI was treated like a parlor trick: Look! It wrote a poem! The second wave was about scale: Look! It can read your entire codebase!

Now we enter the precision wave. 

The question no longer about what it can do. We know it can do almost anything. The question is:

  • How clean is the cut?

  • How deliberate is the design?

  • What’s the philosophy guiding the work?

Because when the tool is this sharp, the onus is on the craftsman.

The Artisan Era

For years, we’ve been waiting for the model to catch up to our ambition. It just did.

Now it’s our turn to decide what we’re building. Not just in function, but in spirit. Not just the “what,” but the “why.”

The Ginsu moment has arrived. The blade is sharp. It’s in our hands now.

How to Design the Soul of an AI Product

When the base model is sharp and stable, the difference between a commodity tool and a memorable product comes down to intentional design.

Here’s a five-step framework to give your AI a soul worth noticing:

1. Choose a north star

What’s the single guiding principle where your AI will never compromise?

  • Accuracy at all costs?

  • Creativity over convention?

  • Empathy above efficiency?

Everything else flows from here.

2. Define its role in the relationship

  • Is it a mentor?

  • A collaborator?

  • A challenger?

  • A sidekick?

This determines not only tone, but when it should lead and when it should defer.

3. Set boundaries

Sharp tools are dangerous without guardrails. Decide early:

  • What topics are out of bounds?

  • What tone is never acceptable?

  • When does it say, “I don’t know”?

4. Craft its voice

Give it linguistic fingerprints:

  • Short, punchy sentences or long, flowing ones?

  • Industry jargon or plain-spoken clarity?

  • Playful metaphor or minimalist precision?

5. Align actions with personality

A soulful AI isn’t just talk. Make sure its behavior matches its stated values:

  • A “precision-first” AI double-checks its own work before answering.

  • A “creative-first” AI surfaces unusual options, even when they’re imperfect.

  • A “mentor” AI explains reasoning as it goes.

Bottom line: GPT-5 is precision waiting for purpose. What you make with it is up to you.

items.title: Rubicon'd
items.description: The legend of John Henry foretells mankind's dwindling economic utility against automation.
items.content:
The legend of John Henry foretells mankind's dwindling economic utility against automation. Then, it was a steam-powered drill decimating the value of human strength. The story ends with Mr. Henry eeking out a momentary victory against the new technology, but then immediately dropping dead, hammer in hand.

The tale symbolizes an era’s end: the industrial revolution steamrolled human Strength and Dexterity as primary labor skills. Machines outpaced muscle - never needing rest. 

Now, in the age of artificial intelligence, we face a new upheaval. 

The steam engine retired John Henry’s hammer. Now we have Einstein in a box! A machine rivaling (quite frequently surpassing) human Intelligence…

So, what do we expect from generative AI? And what should we now expect from ourselves and each other?

There is no going back to how things were. The very definition of “productivity” is changing before our eyes.

Progress has never been a linear path, and productivity isn’t a linear metric. Doubling the speed of work doesn’t simply double the value created. Speed often ignores destination. If you rush in the wrong direction, you just get lost faster. 

Throughout history, each technological leap hasn’t just accelerated work – it has altered the destination. 

What a lone human creates in isolation will inevitably mutate via committee when exposed to more minds (or machines). We see this in co-creation with AI: the outcome of a human working with an AI assistant is fundamentally different from what the human alone would have made. 

Each person’s interaction with AI is unique (almost fractal in its variability) and many traditional corporate structures struggle to comprehend or capitalize on these decentralized, unpredictable workflows. 

Fun fact: over half of employees using AI at work have zero training on its risks or proper use, which shows just how unprepared most organizations are to guide this new reality.

Historically, when machines took over human effort, we adapted by moving up the skill ladder. Raw strength became less valuable when steam shovels and assembly lines arrived. Fine dexterity in handiwork yielded to mechanized precision. 

Society shifted focus to cognitive skills – knowledge, analysis, intelligence. But now AI is besting us on those very skills. 

The hard truth is that knowing things isn’t the prized skill it used to be, not when a machine can know virtually everything. 

As one student aptly noted, today’s AI systems “can access and spit back large swaths of information better than any person.” An AI like ChatGPT can pass standardized exams and regurgitate facts with superhuman efficiency. This means what we typically consider “intelligence” - memorization, rapid recall, routine problem-solving - is no longer a unique human advantage.

Using the Dungeons & Dragons character sheet as a rubric for employment in the modern economy, we’ve seen Strength, Dexterity, and now Intelligence get effectively outsourced to machines. Wisdom then evaporates in a cloud of RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation), reasoning, and synthesized insights.

So, what’s left for humans? 

Our economic utility and marketable skills might boil down to Constitution and Charisma – in other words, our resilience, creativity, adaptability, empathy, and the distinctly human ability to inspire and connect. 

It turns out those “soft” skills are now the hard currency in humanity’s continued employment. 

The jobs AI can’t easily replace are the ones that demand problem-solving, critical thinking, complex communication, creativity, and emotional intelligence - all traits that fall under human charisma and ingenuity. 

We must play to these strengths.

The Power of Questions (Our New Superpower)

If having knowledge is no longer a marketable skill, the new superpower is asking the right questions. 

Framing problems, probing for insight, and steering AI - these are becoming more important than memorizing any formula or fact. In a way, prompting is the new programming. 

Sadly, the traditional American school system hasn’t exactly trained us for this. 

For decades, education emphasized rote memorization and regurgitation of facts - habits that make students act “like robots” doing routine tasks, which actual robots (AI) now do better.

Instead of punishing AI usage, one current student argues, educators should require “more creativity and critical thought – the aspects that separate people from robots.” In other words, curiosity, imagination, and critical inquiry need to move from the margins to the center of our curricula and our workplaces.

It’s ironic: we spent years valuing people for having answers, but now success may hinge on who can ask the more insightful question. 

The ability to brainstorm, to pose an off-the-wall idea, to challenge the default - those are inherently human talents that AI, for all its prowess, doesn’t truly possess. 

AI can output an answer in five seconds, but figuring out which question to ask in the first place remains an art. Our teachers, bosses, and leaders should start nurturing this skill of inquiry. 

After all, an AI is only as good as the prompt it’s given. The future belongs to those who can collaborate with AI, not just consume its answers. And collaboration starts with asking, exploring, and venturing beyond the obvious.

Co-Creation Over Control

To co-create with AI effectively, we’ll need to drop the obsession with micromanagement and rigid control. 

Aiming for ultra-focused, predetermined outcomes will often be a struggle. And it’s likely not the worker’s fault when the bullseye is missed. It might be the fault of management’s rigidity and lack of imagination in defining success.

Granular insistence on conformity through every step of a task (that maligned tradition of micro-management) is likely to be the first casualty of rapid AI adoption. And let’s be honest - who will truly miss that?

Evidence is already bearing this out: in a recent experiment, around 90% of participants improved their performance on a creative task by using generative AI, and those who saw the best improvements were the ones who didn’t try to over-edit or control the AI’s output. 

In contrast, those who clung to a preconceived idea or tried to force the AI into a narrow box gained less. 

The lesson? Give AI room to contribute. 

Don’t treat it like a dumb tool that must be tightly reined in. Co-creation means letting go of a bit of control and trusting a process of give-and-take.

This is a mindset shift for many managers. 

For generations, management has been about enforcing consistency and minimizing variance. But it is folly to hire individuals to think and create, and then expect zero variance in outcome.

With AI in the mix, variance isn’t just a possibility - it’s a guarantee. 

Ten different employees with the same AI tool might solve a problem in ten delightfully different ways. The smartest companies will embrace that diversity of outcomes rather than fear it. 

The role of leadership shifts from directing every move to orchestrating an environment where human-AI teams can experiment, iterate, and surprise you with solutions you hadn’t imagined.

Yes, this requires a leap of faith. Things will break. Not every AI-generated idea will be a good one (or even a coherent one). There will be mistakes and weird tangents. But trying to preemptively eliminate all uncertainty will also eliminate the biggest benefits of AI. 

A rigid organization with edicts for every comma placement will simply smother the creative potential of its human+AI collaborators. In the new era, acceptance and adaptability are the secret sauce. 

In fact, business experts note that adopting generative AI is such a massive change that leaders must help people use the tech “in the right way, for the right tasks” and then “continually adjust and adapt” as the technology evolves. 

In other words, continuous learning and flexibility aren’t just feel-good slogans - they’re now requirements for survival. 

Companies that empower their teams to iteratively learn with AI will leap ahead. Those that cling to old command-and-control habits will watch opportunities pass them by at lightspeed.

Embrace the New Journey

So, no, we will not be returning to how things were. Not back to the old industrial workflows - not even to last year’s way of doing things. 

There’s no returning to a world where human workers could coast on repetitive tasks or cookie-cutter job descriptions. 

AI isn’t a temporary fad or just another productivity tool. It’s a whole new collaborator on the team, one that changes the very nature of our expected destination. 

Where we’re going is new, different, and altogether unique. Uncharted territory. 

Each of us is now primed for our own unique journey with these intelligent machines. The smartest businesses will embrace this, will nurture and accelerate the awakening of human potential that happens when employees are free to co-create with AI.

This is a rallying cry to embrace co-creation. 

We should cheer the end of the mindless production-line mentality and welcome a future where imagination and adaptability rule. It’s time to re-imagine job roles, expectations, and outcomes with a spirit of curiosity. 

Rather than fearing an AI “takeover,” think of it as an invitation to rediscover what makes human work meaningful. We have the chance to redesign work itself to be more engaging, letting machines handle the drudgery while we focus on insight, strategy, and connection.

Remember, the heroes of tomorrow aren’t those who can memorize the most facts or crank out the most widgets - AI has that covered. 

The heroes will be those who can chart a new path, ask the questions no one else thought to ask, and unite teams (human and machine) toward creative goals. 

So ask yourself (and ask your AI): what can we discover today that wasn’t possible yesterday? In a world where “knowing things” is cheap, the value lies in vision, judgment, and yes, charisma.

There is no return to the old normal, and that’s okay. We’re forging a new normal as we speak. Forward is the only available direction now.

Embrace the detours and unexpected outcomes along the way.

In this unprecedented journey of human and AI co-evolution, we are all adventurers. And the traits every adventurer needs in abundance is the Constitution to keep going and the Charisma to inspire others to join.

The road ahead is uncertain and exciting, and it belongs to those who are ready to create, not those who cling to the past. Onward, there is no looking back.


—

items.title: G(ai)ve it away
items.description: The internet was never for us.
items.content:
The internet was never for us. We were for the internet. We’re not its users, we’re its fuel.

A recurring type of post appears on my LinkedIn news feed: Gainfully employed creative professionals announcing their plans to remove all personal work from the internet. This self-immolation gets credited as the best fight against Generative AI’s ever-improving performance.

Yes, it’s true, the internet as we know it is fueled by our contributions. This is the value proposition that’s been a mainstay since the mid-nineties. We give over our individual perspectives - our creations - and we gain visibility for our work from friends, family, and total strangers. Exposure to a global audience at our fingertips, in our pockets, drives us to share - to be seen - to be perceived - to give it all away.

Those same companies offering that free space for us to upload our creations recently found a new way to interpret the terms-of-service agreement. We’re no longer just a commodity of eyeballs that see ads. We’re a highly moderated training source for the ever-growing Generative AI frontier models.

Now, perhaps we should rightly conjure ire about the injustices of our work being “trained upon” without explicit agreement between parties. Yet, let’s not forget just how many artists across history died penniless, only to be discovered as talent posthumously.

Are we so drunk on the capitalistic exchange as to assume our work is immediately valuable? And would a Spotify-style compensation of few cents per month be the best that we hope to gain from this transaction?

How could any of us divvy out an appropriate fractional creation credit for anything we make? …especially for those of us with skills derived from any structured education! The countless museum visits, magazine spreads, movies and music that we’ve all “trained upon” make each of us fluid collages, distilled aggregates of all we’ve digested.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

However, there's a crucial distinction: while we draw inspiration from others, we don't directly replicate or monetize another's unique style en masse, which is something AI models can do.

In early internet days, presenting any creation to persist online was far more of an undertaking. Someone needed a desire to plunk around online for a few hours, learning a little code, and ending up with a basic Geocities site. A few blurbs, a few grainy pics, a few animating GIFs... The dripping blood divider bar was a personal favorite:

But as the years rolled on, the ability to create and share online became easier - with increased fidelity and ever expanding reach! The barrier to share with a global audience evaporated. Each of us had the potential to attract the world’s attention.

Incredible new perspectives arose naturally in our feeds. New expressions, new mediums, new messages. We began to find ourselves in each other. Some found ways to monetize that exchange. A select few could even live off of it.

And so we find ourselves here now: In a time where sharing anything online explicitly means contributing to a new synthetic form of professional competition. We’re now in a time where our collective history of shared creations online, our decades of documented experiences, are all hoovered up into a system that will digest and abstract it into a technicolor digital slurry. 

And generative AI sits - waiting - ready for anyone to suggest compiling any idea into reality - using that slurry to help realize the unique request for a collage of words, sounds, visuals, actions.

This new reality makes complex creation available to those without much skill in whichever chosen medium for that output. It’s no surprise to see established artists cry foul.

Those who have already found commercial success in monetizing each voyage over the barrier of creativity. Charging for an ability to realize those unique requests into that same collection of collages.

Conjuring expression into reality on command put those talented few in rarefied air. Artists casually vault over a barrier that so many cannot fathom traversing themselves. The average person either lacks skills, or carries an abundance of self-doubt preventing the allocation of any effort or time to sharpen those skills themselves.

That barrier was previously a convenient monetizable endpoint in the freewheeling days of sharing literally everything online. “Here. Look. Do you like what I do? Hire me!” That’s how I got my start in my career… Demo reels, portfolio websites, clippings, the whole shebang.

The bitter pill: we’ve already agreed to give it all away.

The necessary wording was in our terms of service agreement from the start, however vague it may have been. Go ahead, read the fine print on any social site. We allow the forfeiture of sole ownership rights to everything posted on those sites.

Instagram shares ownership of your posted work. Or, it at least has the right to republish, even repurpose and earn money on all of your work shared there. Facebook always stated as much. Why do you think it’s free to post there? 

Yet, these stipulations generally grant rights to the platform itself, not to third parties using the content for purposes like training AI models without the creators' explicit consent.

Artists should have the right to control how their work is used and rescind consent to their creations training AI models, especially when it could impact their livelihood. The controversy arises because using their work in AI training should exceed the scope of what they agreed to, raising ethical and legal concerns about intellectual property rights.

What this means now is that fewer people will need the creative services offered by others because these machines have activated a newfound fidelity to everyone’s innate perspective. It is creativity distilled without the need for skill, time or ability. All that’s needed is a unique perspective and a decent description of what you want to see.

Again, I must say: I am one of these people who made a living for the past 20 years as a creative. I’ve sold my ability to cross that creativity barrier to companies large and small. My livelihood got disrupted this year due to the quest for “operational efficiencies.” I am among the constituencies of those who cry foul.

I’m just saying “foul” is not the right thing to cry at this moment.

Perhaps instead we should recognize that legal frameworks need to evolve alongside technology to adequately safeguard creators' rights.

It's notable that artists are among the first to experience significant disruption due to AI, serving as "canaries in the coal mine" for the broader workforce. Our situation highlights how automation can affect even those professions that were once thought to be uniquely human and creativity-driven.

The professional goalposts for creatives not only shifted, they collided with the three-point line and the outfield wall. This game we must now play is new, and it’s a mashed-up abstraction of disciplines.

But perhaps this is an opportunity. Artists are uniquely positioned to use their creativity to highlight and interpret the impacts of AI on society. By incorporating these themes into our work, we can help others grasp the complexities of technological advancement and its effects on human labor.

The level of sensory engagement any of us can now present is astounding. Given the desire, we can create a near-perfect representation of whatever we’re imagining. For better or worse...

So, I recommend we get good at reading the fine print of our chosen distribution platforms, and dive into the newly emerging next iteration of the internet and see what can be seen. Make what might be made - with skilled hands and a keen editorial eye.

In embracing these new tools, we can create work that both reflects and informs public understanding. This opens up new avenues for artistic expression that both critique and shape the discourse around AI and creativity.

So let's not just adapt; let's lead. After all, who better than artists to navigate and define this new landscape?

items.description: It’s always the same.
items.content:
It’s always the same. New faces appear in the town square. Boisterous voices claiming the impossible. Something about the pitch always sounds downright unbelievable - and the peddlers agree that you’re right to think it sounds just as incredible as your disbelief demands.

But, of course, you’re wrong - because this one is different... This one is industry-leading, clinically-proven, world-renowned, and your reluctance is just a byproduct of your own ignorance. You see, your competition is clamoring, your customers are migrating, your business needs exactly what we’re selling!

What’s old is new again. Generative AI is a technology that is just opaque enough, fanciful enough, to entice via wonder just as easily as it does with fear.

You see, before now we had a consistent trajectory with technology. It was governed by a concept called Moore’s Law. Something that has remained an unwavering constant since the 1960s: The doubling of computer power every two years.

Now? Well, now it’s a little different. Moore’s law has received an exponent on that growth. That doubling previously arriving every two years - it’s now here every six months.

And with that acceleration comes wave after wave of hype and fly-by-night promises.

It’s hard for anyone to keep up on the relevant and legitimate abilities of any new technology, and Generative AI (Gen AI) is eclipsing itself weekly. So, it’s understandable that the current sales pitches for Gen AI apps and tools include a heightened level of urgency along with the blue-sky hand-waving optimism of incredible efficiency gains.

Two opposing, yet symbiotic camps emerge in the SMB x Gen AI space

But first we need to touch on the concept of an API key: It’s basically a handshake between computer programs.

Think of the company you’ve solicited as the one opening the door for you to access another company’s technology. The wrapper placed around the API (Application Programming Interface) is your interface that the third-party service created for you. From there you can adjust and control that foundational technology, Gen AI.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

Now, the first camp consists of third-party services hooked into the APIs of major foundational-model providers. This camp offers quick efficiency gains but often remains hazy on the details. 

The second camp comprises SMBs that might be confused or downright fearful of the technology, hesitant to adopt it due to uncertainty and lack of understanding.

These two camps are inadvertently feeding into one another, creating a cycle of hype and apprehension - which then feeds the attention economy, fueling the entrenchment of each camp.

So, let’s break down what’s at the heart of this

There’s a handful of companies with the resources available to train foundational models, these are what we’d call Generative AI.

OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta, Anthropic, Mistral, and a few other major players are those able to piece together the massive compute clusters used to accumulate (and synthesize) the data that is necessary to forge a frontier model. At the time of this writing we could agree this classification is most easily described as ChatGPT.

API keys are available for a monthly fee to third-party businesses to then create tools making use of that foundational technology. The foundational services like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT’s API allow those businesses to offer any value-added sales pitch that their product-marketing team dares to conjure. 

The FTC is light-years behind on figuring out how to regulate any of these claims, and nowhere near ready to require adequate and upfront privacy messaging.

Here’s the issue with that

When all you’re sold is access to a completely different company’s offering, the pitch had better sound downright magical. In fact, some businesses, like Canva, literally call their Gen AI offerings magic!

And if you’re not striking a contract directly with a foundational model provider - OpenAI, Google, et al. - you remain beholden to the same security afforded to all API-key holders. Like the one that any third-party company is using. 

Those intermediary companies don’t have the deep pockets that are required to negotiate a Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policy.

Without a ZDR policy in place, this is likely where things would run afoul for your PII and SI handling policies. Don’t allow third-party apps and tools access to any Personally Identifying Information and Sensitive Information of either your business and your customers without clarity on ZDR.

This means do not use any Gen AI tool or app with customer data, sensitive meeting notes, financial documents, or anything you wouldn’t want mistaken as public knowledge about your business or clients.

It’s often necessary to transmit that sensitive business and customer information to deliver on those magical benefits of many sales pitches by third-party Gen AI apps and tools. And that includes companies like Zoom offering meeting summaries. The major enterprise organizations do not use that function, explicitly because of the loose data-retention policies.

I’ve seen upstarts of all sizes offer customer data management tools like CRMs that are supposedly supercharged with Gen AI. …please be cautious when approaching this type of sales pitch.

Allowing third parties access to your data runs afoul of your business’ commitment to the privacy of your customers. It runs afoul of your business’ commitment to itself! Yet this privacy consideration is often buried in the fine print. And we all know how time consuming it is to digest that kind of legalese. Summarizing that policy before signing anything becomes crucially important. 

Thankfully, that type of summation is an easy task for Gen AI! 

My goal here is to shrink the divide between promise and reality as we navigate through what’s coming next. I want to calm the nerves of those who might be confused about where to begin. 

Demystifying the concepts surrounding Gen AI helps reduce fear by providing clear, accurate information. Simultaneously, tempering enthusiasm and watering down the hype ensures that businesses make informed decisions rather than succumbing to unrealistic promises. 

By educating SMBs on both the capabilities and limitations of Gen AI, we can foster a more balanced and effective adoption of this technology.

To bridge the gap between the third-party service providers and the apprehensive SMBs, a structured framework for understanding and implementing Gen AI is necessary. This includes clear guidelines on data privacy, realistic expectations of what Gen AI can achieve, and ongoing support to ensure successful integration.

By adopting this balanced approach, businesses can harness the true potential of Gen AI without falling prey to the pitfalls of either blind enthusiasm or crippling fear. This not only promotes sustainable growth but also builds trust and reliability in the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence.

So, for those interested - I offer workshops for SMB owners and their teams to learn the basics and dive into practical applications. I’m also available for one-on-one meetings to talk through what’s possible for your business and industry. Please inquire at cwilke@fellowvector.com, or book time through our website: fellowvector.com.
