items.title: Shame to see it
items.description: Lazy, uneven adoption of advanced AI tooling only hurts those you serve.
items.content:
We've all experienced the frustration of interacting with a poorly designed chatbot or being stuck in an endless loop of automated phone menus.

Calls are often diverted to prolonged queues, eventually reaching a single overburdened support individual—and I stress, individual—who is buried under a never-ending queue of increasingly frustrated customers.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

We shouldn’t attempt to do more with less without the augmentation of modern technology, tools, and processes. ​​The old ways don't need to die or even suffer, but they can’t expect to gain the process optimizations afforded to us by Gen AI.

“I didn’t get that… Can you repeat yourself?”

Without incorporating the foundational shifts brought about by these technologies, attempts to streamline business operations will only tax the remaining individuals employed within the organization - those so frequently referenced as family.

The classic saying: you can’t have your cake and eat it too - might help reveal the fallacy gripping those eager to hop on the lucrative wave of modern productivity. If businesses want to streamline, downsize, or supercharge their operations, they have to take a bold leap into incorporating modern technologies like Generative Artificial Intelligence.

Sure, it's scary, but trying to boost productivity while merely cutting headcount just hurts your remaining workforce and those they serve. 

This push for automation and operational efficiencies isn’t just raising the bar for achieving a comfortable life; it's removing the lowest rung altogether. The middle class—often considered the backbone of the economy—is being eroded as technology replaces roles that were once secure pathways to stable employment. 

According to a report by the Brookings Institution, automation threatens up to 25% of jobs in the United States, disproportionately affecting middle-income positions. Some even predict a global job loss of around 230 million jobs in the next two years.

As technology transitions from being ubiquitous to omnipresent and soon to ephemeral, we're witnessing a cycle where advancements rapidly replace their predecessors, leaving little lasting value. Die-hard devotion dissolved in the great footrace to genericity. And being generic means competing with generic clones. Q-tips, Jello, Kleenex, Band-Aid all ubiquitous, but generic equivalents are just as good.

This rapid cycle erodes the lasting value that these individual technologies bring to our lives - and Generative AI is accelerating the sense of instability in the job market among highly skilled workers not used to this level of persistent uncertainty.

A Personal Reflection

I find myself as a testament to this shift. The last project I worked on involved developing a vector database for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with a Large Language Model (LLM) wrapper—a cutting-edge application of AI technology. Yet, in a twist of irony, I helped build the very tool that contributed to my underemployment.

In April, "operational efficiencies" landed on my head. I've been underemployed ever since. I feel like I helped build the gun that shot me in the back of the head. This experience has profoundly influenced my thoughts on the advancement of technology and its impact on jobs.

The hollowing out of the human interface in areas where we spend our money and focus our attention is a significant issue. Businesses are increasingly automating services, but the personal touch that fosters trust and loyalty is getting lost. Customers often feel frustrated when they can't reach a real person to resolve complex issues, damaging brand reputation and customer satisfaction in the long run.

Also, the over-reliance on technology without adequate human support creates a fragile environment. Frequent internet interruptions these days could render someone unemployable or drive a business bankrupt - underscoring how heavily we've come to rely on technology for basic functioning and livelihood.

Technology Eating Itself

The rapid advancement of technology is, in a way, eating itself. Just look at the level of bespoke creation we're capable of with AI already! We're witnessing the diminishing economic viability for human input in creative and analytical tasks. This not only affects employment but also raises questions about the lasting intrinsic value of human labor.

Generative AI as a concept is souring amongst many. No small portion are "classical" business owners. Some hate it, some are confused by it, some are scared of it. There's not too many explorers left in the crowd.

Generative AI and other advanced technologies should be seen as tools to augment human capabilities, not replace them entirely… And it absolutely shouldn’t be the basis to severely hamstring and overwork the remaining few after the decision to implement any operational efficiency.

For instance, AI-driven chatbots can handle routine inquiries, freeing up human support staff to tackle more complex issues that require empathy and critical thinking. And treat the skills of empathy and critical thinking as wildly valuable - compensate accordingly.

And while we’re at it. Don’t fill those remaining few who are “good” at their job with a plate full of work that would make anyone scream. Staff accordingly, compensate accordingly.

By maintaining a strong human interface, companies can benefit from technology without eroding the middle class, widening socioeconomic gaps, or damaging the trust and satisfaction of the consumers enticed to engage with the product or service.

The incentive to automate is present, clearly - but the process to integrate it remains vague and opaque for many business owners. And from the employee perspective - many have already felt the impact of operational efficiencies firsthand, leading to underemployment and uncertainty.

It's high time businesses took a bold leap into modern technology—but responsibly. By integrating advanced technologies like Generative AI in a way that augments rather than replaces human roles, companies can achieve operational efficiencies without sacrificing customer satisfaction or employee well-being.

The future doesn't have to be a choice between embracing technology and preserving jobs. With a balanced approach, we can leverage technological advancements to enhance human capabilities, maintain the middle class, and ensure lasting value in our increasingly digital world.

It's a real shame to see the current trend, but it's not too late to change course. Businesses must recognize that they can't have their cake and eat it too. They need to invest in modern technology thoughtfully, keeping the human element at the core of their operations.

items.title: Our return to active discovery
items.description: For the past two decades, we’ve siphoned joy from the effervescent glow of our content-delivering algorithms.
items.content:
For the past two decades, we’ve siphoned joy from the effervescent glow of our content-delivering algorithms. Personalized feeds and up-next recommendations created a customized media pipeline that easily beat out advertising’s classic, but outdated sifting strategies.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

However, as Generative AI emerges, we find ourselves at the dawn of a new era—one where passive consumption now gives way to active discovery, bringing both immense potential and significant risks.

Long ago, the golden age of marketing operated on a spray and pray methodology. The assumption was demographics cared about certain programming so advertisers would plunk their penny in that program’s pond. This meant waiting and wishing someone who cared saw that personally relevant marketing message and heeded that specific call to action.

The foggy math required to extrapolate direct value of that ad placement teetered on snake oil. Nothing quantifiable about it, in fact, it was aggressively opaque in its subjective effectiveness.

It was hard to attract the right eyeballs. Even harder keeping them focused on the pitch. And nearly impossible to verify purchases made from that group. But still, each sale was earned, each product pitch was intentional.

Take music for example. Long ago, it was seen as peculiar to hoard music. Few of us could live like John Cusack in High Fidelity – dedicating the majority of his living space to physical media.

In reality, music was a sparing expense using dollars we scraped together to earn the joy of buying new content. It was a time honored ritual – go to the music store, peel off the cellophane, take that first whiff of the printed smell of fresh liner notes.

But this wasn’t just a transaction; it was a deeply personal experience. Each album purchase carried the weight of careful consideration, and the emotional resonance of the music was heightened by the effort invested in acquiring it.

In the past twenty years, music discovery shifted dramatically. New music is algorithmically slotted into playlists that are statistically most likely to be accessed by the desired user. New music arrives - sometimes completely unbeknownst to the listener.

Sure, this is great for stats like play counts, but does the reception of that new musical expression make the same impact on the listener?

I argue it doesn’t.

The convenience of algorithmically delivered discovery dulled the emotional resonance that once came with the ritual of media consumption. A ritual that cherished the slow burn of anticipation and the deliberate act of choosing. Now, we face an endless barrage of content that demands little of us but time.

This shift signified more than just a change in the way we discover music—it reflected a broader trend of passive consumption replacing active engagement.

The fading algorithmic grip on our attention

The effective capitalistic utility of algorithmic content delivery was designed to satisfy increasingly atomized individual whims. Spray and pray fell to big data’s certainty.

But that era of content delivery is now giving way to a more active form of information discovery. We decried many generations for being self-involved—egotistical, self-absorbed. Yet still, we built algorithms to feed that same quirk of humanity. GenAI, however, now offers a pivotal shift.

As we transition from self-obsessed to self-propelled, we are presented with a seemingly magical tool to dig into any topic, and retrieve any information instantly.

This shift marks the beginning of a new era where the boundaries of knowledge are now pushed by individuals, not institutions. Our thirst for new knowledge, which has always driven human progress, now finds itself in a digital playground with fewer limits and greater risks.

Institutions see this as dangerous. Governments, schools, corporations and religions all now must grapple with an unchained super-intelligence guiding each of us to discover, devour and digest new information on any subject we desire. Guardrails have yet to arrive and the scramble is on to prevent wholesale institutional collapse.

As we individually explore, surely we’ll come across something we shouldn’t. Curiosity becomes piqued when we find a locked door, and a siren call of intrigue can still attract those listening. This means that our attention can become focused like a laser beam on areas we’re not supposed to discover.

If inquisitive folks surround restricted topics from every angle, how long before the exact outline of off-limits topics becomes clear as day? If our clarity and speed of discovery allow us to trace the contours of verboten data, how difficult will it be to synthesize the relevance of off-limit topics purely based on where they exist within the massive vector-retrieval data lake?

As it’s been said: the absence of data is still data. And contextually speaking, the relative relationship of that blacked out area of data might be all we need to infer much of the information deemed too sensitive to share.

Our individual ability to define the undefined isn’t so scary if we remain individuals. But as a collective force, we’ll need a compelling reason to halt digging into certain topics. And relying on because-I-said-so illegality will not prevent intrigue from spreading like the virality that marketers wished to achieve just a decade ago.

The power of curiosity should not be underestimated. It is the same force that once drove explorers to the edges of maps and now propels us all to the corners of the internet.

GenAI, in its essence, is a double-edged sword—democratizing information while also opening doors to places we might have once considered too dangerous or taboo to explore.

These contemporary, ubiquitos media platforms altered the very fabric of our interactions. They eroded our sense of self. While expanding our networks, we’ve reduced relationships to transactions rather than genuine connections.

But that energy of our desire must go somewhere. So the need for connection drives us deeper into the information we covet. The natural force of entropy demands it. How else do we create the hierarchy required to maintain any niche community?

As communities grow and fragment, the information they produce and consume becomes increasingly chaotic, subject to the unpredictable forces of individual interests and societal pressures. Consider the heightened level of toxicity within super fandoms like Star Wars, politics and cultural-critique one-upmanship. Echo chambers emerge and create dangerous polarization where only tepid interest once reigned.

This entropy reflects a broader cultural shift where the pursuit of knowledge became less about collective enlightenment and more about individual status. It’s a rat race. Incentivized play - which is just work hiding within that false flashes of easy dopamine delivery.

The more popular a community, the more fervent its base, the more extraction becomes necessary to assert social status within that community. Ever increasing monetization creates a vacuum chamber for devotion and an ad-hoc caste system emerges through exploiting individual status jockeying.

After all, it’s happened before. Remember Beanie Babies?

In this transformative era, GenAI is already redefining education, entertainment and information retrieval. But this newfound superpower comes with a twist…

We can now offload the tedium of packaging of our thoughts to GenAI. The ravings of the lunatic on that city corner can immediately become polished, coherent narratives. This superpower now also risks homogenizing ideas, crystalizing motives, and making eloquence accessible while potentially stripping our communication of its depth and originality.

This democratization of eloquence could lead to a world where the substance of ideas is overshadowed by their polished presentation. Think of it like making all ideas taste like chicken. The flavor profile of batshit crazy will match that of Nobel laureates.

As our communities fractalize, each of us gain more control of our unique ship. Some may wander befuddled, treading circles around their comfort zone, but many will seek and explore. The pitfall in that increasingly individual pursuit become perilous as our ability to discern had already been eroded by the ease and comfort of global algorithms vetting the content we digest.

As we move from past practices to present challenges, with curiosity as our compass and GenAI as our navigator, we are venturing into uncharted territories of thought and expression.

Sanity can now get applied to ideas as easily as spellcheck to any missive, decree or manifesto. The ramblings of incoherent thought can gain coherence with the help of GenAI, but at what cost? And how do we identify ravings from reason when it all sounds so damn convincing?

The boundaries we set today will define the information landscape of tomorrow. But in this rapidly changing terrain, the rigidity of these boundaries may clash with the fluidity of human curiosity and creativity. Our humanity—our ability to question, to feel, and to connect—remains our most valuable guide.

So, as we step into this new era of active discovery, we must steel ourselves from the onslaught of discordant ideas slipping into our view with polished sales pitches that we haven’t seen in decades. Sales pitches we’re no longer accustomed to filter out as noise.

items.content:
Don’t blink - or you’ll miss this brief window of time where you can confidently identify AI-generated work.

Fingers, teeth, eating spaghetti, all the blatant telltale signs of artificially generated images are getting ironed out and smoothed to a high-gloss lacquer sheen.

Those pithy turns of phrase so routinely found in text generations will evaporate. The agents answering the phone calls for customer support will remain friendly and functional, while imperceptibly shifting to LLM-powered voice assistants.

A growing array of this technology’s applications are surpassing any reasonable uncanny-valley threshold. Each will be quietly A/B tested - proving consumer preference.

Take capitalism’s most recent trounce through the tulips: Generative AI employed to manifest a new origin story for the zombie toy store Toys ‘r’ Us.

Commentary aside on fictionalized/romanticized origins of brands destroyed by private equity firms - this wonky fever dream of an advertisement fantastically highlights our current moment’s true democratization of spectacle.

Let’s not forget that the past decade of peak summer blockbuster tent-poles quickly devolved all third-act resolutions into crumble porn. This choice eroded mass-market representations of average human experiences. Instead leaning into the raw spectacle of climax after climax reducing city blocks to frilly confetti falling in slow-motion during brooding fights between good and evil.

But now, John Q. Public can also create this level of spectacle with no new hardware required.

Obviously, the mainstream content machine cries foul. Calling this the death of spectacle - just because we can conjure such imagery ourselves in the palms of our hands.

Turns out we can now employ this similar level of spectacle grandeur when processing slow-motion trots of our pooch in the back yard on freshly fallen Nebraska snow.

And while this might sound benign, I recognize the implications: This is the wholesale destruction of digital certainty.

Each person with a smart phone now has access to professional-grade tools of deception.

So, how do we gather enough information about our reality to verify it’s genuine? …not just information slipped into our algorithmic data feeds that, we’re all ashamed to admit, really do drive our perceptions of the tangible reality around us.

A tailored reality is nothing new. But Generative AI’s capabilities to wholesale create a digital-twin marionette of anyone (with mere seconds of visual and audio source data) will expose all of our deep-seated feelings towards our fellow humans.

Generative AI forces us to accept that others will not be able to identify the distinction between real life and a bespoke, personally deceptive digital facsimile.

Capitalism asks, “what real harm is there in a legendary sports broadcaster consenting to NBC’s AI-generated Olympic broadcast recaps using his voice and persona?” Next to none.

The harm is when someone decides to use this technology to clone your loved one’s voice and call you urgently requesting bail money.

So, who are we to be in this process?

If everything now becomes possible to anyone trained or otherwise, why not explore our expression within all these mediums that we’d previously only ever admired?

Why do we believe we’re not worthy of creative expression in mediums we haven’t trained to use well enough for economic utility?

Painters don’t generally forage for pigments to create their own paint colors. They don’t generally harvest horsehair, wood and metal to craft their own paint brushes.

I’m a professional writer, but I don’t craft an ax to level my own trees to pulp the wood to create parchment as a medium to carry my words. Hell, these words may never actually get printed on any physical medium!

These are all just bits and bytes floating in the nebulous electronic ether. Some call it “The Cloud” others call it “The Net” but what of this truly exists?

And should any of what I’ve made here exist? Is there an objective delineation between right-speak and foul-mouthed lunacy? Pugnaciously created art and the abomination of computer-assisted creation?

Yeah, it’s understandable being mad right now. The barrier to creation is removed. The toil and talent that once divided the makers from the market has dissolved into a mere nice-to-have. This change is wildly frustrating to those who banked on that barrier for any modicum of commercial returns.

Suddenly those capable of monetizing the voyage over that barrier have lost all economic utility in that skill. Myself included.

So, where do I direct my ire?

And what do I do when I can’t monetize my assistance through that level of abstraction? When the value I held to create suddenly evaporates?

And what was I truly gatekeeping with my marketable skill? The ability to tangibly manifest expression?

If generative AI can democratize creation and remove previously-necessary layers of abstraction to allow interaction with raw expression, who am I to cry foul?

After all, who are we if not embodied manifestations of expression? And if everyone can now express with full fidelity, can’t we just share our expressions and grow from there?

items.description: I admit that all these tech hype cycles have been exhausting.
items.content:
I admit that all these tech hype cycles have been exhausting. As an employee of the tech sector, I’ve had a front-row seat to Big Tech’s response to each new wave of potentially life-altering technology.

This post originally appeared on Lozafina’s community blog. Republished here with permission.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

It’s understandable that most folks might have tuned out somewhere between news of NFTs (non-fungible tokens), bitcoins, and metaverses booming and busting all over their social feeds. Most of those have been obnoxiously over-hyped.

Now, Artificial Intelligence - or more specifically, Generative AI - takes center stage. This one is unlike the fleeting trends of Bored Ape NFTs selling for millions, or Mark Zuckerberg’s radical metaverse. Generative AI promises (and threatens) to more profoundly reshape our world. 

But before we dive into the potential future, let's unpack Generative AI as a concept.

Generative AI is an umbrella term that refers to algorithms that can create new content. Specifically, content like text, images, music, or even entire videos.

In fact, as you read, please note that bold-italic text represents surviving novel ChatGPT-generated passages - not to mention every image in this article.

We should all be familiar with the concept of algorithms serving up existing content:

  • Google search algorithms

  • Social and news feed algorithms

  • Related TV shows and up-next algorithms

  • Spotify’s entire music platform is built around cultivating music to fit your data-driven interests. 

All these simple incarnations of Artificial Intelligence only serve up existing content.

Now, with Generative AI, all that personalized information, once used to serve relevant existing information, can be the context used to generate brand new content to be spun up to keep your attention. This means that machines learn from existing data and now use that knowledge to produce something entirely new - from crunching numbers to creating art, literature, even entire TV channels.

Does GenAI steal from existing work?

The most straightforward answer I can give at this moment is that we just don’t know yet.

Multiple court cases are underway that will help give some legal precedent to set foundational context. Currently, the most high profile case is NYT vs OpenAI. The case isn’t very cut and dry, but thankfully Generative AI is fantastic at summarization. Please enjoy a brief overview of this ongoing legal battle, courtesy of Perplexity.ai.

The way these systems digest information when training the foundational AI models is very similar to how a human learns about a subject. Generalization, summarization and categorization of training data is really all that’s left from the original content. The actual trove of information would be far too big to keep at top of mind for any LLM (Large Language Model) or human, for that matter.

I’d describe GenAI’s outputs as a techno-collage – complex mosaics of colors, concepts, ideas, perspectives, decades of culture and style – distilled and recontextualized.

Using this definition, there’s strong potential for GenAI’s output to be classified as unique works deserving of copyright.

The other major question…. Will it take my job?

Generative AI is surprising everyone - even those who invented it. Novel knowledge emerges from making connections between points of massive amounts of data. This means the AI can think new thoughts, reach conclusions, and generate novel insights that aren’t included in its original training data.

So, yes, that is to say that Generative AI is proving to be quite capable of automating remarkably complex tasks. Many of those same tasks that would make up most, if not all, of just about anyone’s job duties.

The worry for some, and expectation for others, is that AI will take over both manual labor as well as white-collar jobs.

The Industrial Revolution's impact on manual labor by automated machines led to massive social and economic upheavals. The transition was painful and chaotic, but also created entirely new job sectors.

Fast forward to the present, and we're facing a similar disruption. AI is capable of performing tasks that were quite recently the sole domain of humans—data analysis, customer service, even content creation.

Clerical tasks, administrative departments, bookkeeping, HR, marketing, even sales departments are at risk of complete automation! There just aren’t many tasks performed in these departments that couldn’t be automated through a series of Generative AI tools.

So businesses will learn to do more with less – most will hire fewer people moving forward and dismiss any further need for entry level positions.

But, doesn’t GenAI lie sometimes?

It does. These errors are called hallucinations, so calling them lies might make them sound a bit more deceptive than they are. The nature of generating an output usually requires the AI to thrust one foot in front of the other, word after word, until it’s completed its response.

Speaking extemporaneously and with conviction about any prompted subject is how LLMs function. Needless to say, some outputs won’t pass the sniff test. Those rates are drastically decreasing with each iterative release, but there’s always going to be a non-zero chance that the machine is lying to you.

However, the gains to business productivity that AI promises are too great, even with the occasional whoopsie. After all, we’ve trusted people to do all the jobs, and look at what a mess we’ve made of this place.

My greatest fear is how we decide to adopt this technology into our existing workflows. Perhaps a human in a position of power relies on the wisdom of this sage machine to make consequential decisions. A hallucination with this context could become a life-or-death error.  And, with that said, it should come as no surprise that the healthcare insurance industry is adopting AI to replace humans in the wake of turbulent layoffs.

Is this giving you a vision of a hellish future of weaponized bureaucracy with no oversight, no insight, and no recourse? …you’re not alone.

The sobering reality is the jobs market will continue to restrict. We’ll go from conventional employment agreements to a market filled with patchworking, hopscotching, enterprising individuals.

We’ve seen glimmers of it in the so-called gig economy, but those examples were just gigs in employment’s clothing with centralized owners of distribution and dispatch having complete command over work performed. That’s not where we’re headed. What comes next is chaotic and disruptive, but ultimately empowering.

New jobs, new opportunities, new livelihoods are all waiting for us to create them.

This transformation will feel abrupt – and uncomfortable – but we’ve been uncomfortable for ages now. We’re built for this.

We’ll need to reskill. Thankfully, that’s as simple as using a friendly conversational interface. 

My advice? Talk to it.

We must also choose to accept GenAI as an ally instead of an intruder. It may not come to take our current jobs, but someone using it just might.

Adopting GenAI into our lives, understanding its uses and limitations will give us a chance to live more vibrantly - communicate more clearly - understand and be understood without delay. The interpersonal potential of Generative AI is vast and largely untapped. From revolutionizing creative processes to solving complex global tensions, its applications are endless.

The story of AI doesn’t have to remain one of tech giants cutting jobs with cutting-edge research. It can be a story of human ingenuity and the individual’s quest to push collective boundaries.

items.title: Value is myth
items.description: We orchestrate our lives around myths of all sizes.
items.content:
We orchestrate our lives around myths of all sizes. Our chosen belief systems, hierarchical structures, punishments and rewards — even our delineation between good and evil stems from myth.

Myth is not a concept to be mocked, it’s vitally important to our society’s continued function. However, I see an alarming trend where positions of power attempt to apply their own universal or objective truth to the concept of value.

But value isn’t a concrete concept. Not in and of itself, and not across categories.

Value is not a commodity — it’s the result of a process. And even then, depending on perspective that process should be valued differently.

Think about the distinction between news and marketing: news is something someone else doesn’t want to share and marketing is something you don’t particularly care to hear.

Its obvious that news is the more valuable information type, but things turn on their head when the economic-expansion zealots of corporate America (including the exported variety) get involved in that proposition.

After all, how could we consistently, without fail, achieve value in countless industries with unique and specific OKRs (Objectives & Key Results)? And how could those results all possibly carry an intrinsic value?

Results-focused action pursues optimal outcomes with minimal input. Do it at scale and that’s enterprise in a nutshell. And as far as results go, there’s nothing sweeter than those three little letters: ARR—Annual Recurring Revenue.

items.title: The space between
items.description: Generative AI's goldmine lay in the hands of generalists.
items.content:
Much ado is made about SMEs—Subject Matter Experts. Those with a depth of knowledge on specific subjects are among the most sought after in the professional world. However, I believe the truly transformative value is found in the space between these knowledge islands.

Note: Unique AI-generated phrases are presented as bold and italic.

How does the 'space between' function? Isn’t it just dead space?

Well, technically, it’s called latent space—a term drawn from machine learning which refers to the semantic relationship between nodes of knowledge. Latent space is not empty; rather, it is rich with potential, awaiting activation.

Think about it this way. When I say “fuzzy puppy,” you can’t help but visualize a fuzzy puppy, but surely you’ve imagined a specific breed. Was it a Labrador, a Husky, or maybe a German Shepherd? Your individual latent space generated additional context when prompted using information from your lived experience.

Sound familiar?

Prompt engineering is essentially the trendy buzzword packaging that describes the process of activating a model’s latent space. It's the Renaissance art of the digital age, where the spaces between known quantities hold the secrets to new forms of expression and discovery.

Our abstraction from our learned experience leads to us synthesize new ideas by generating meaningful representations and contextual coherence within emerging scenarios. Or more simply put: we experience, we reflect, and we act. Much like an LLM uses its distilled representations of training data to create novel outputs.

Historically, the most significant breakthroughs often occurred at the intersection of diverse fields. Consider the Enlightenment, a period marked by an explosion of knowledge across disciplines. Philosophers like Francis Bacon and René Descartes didn’t confine themselves to narrow specialties but rather explored the space between to forge new methodologies and philosophies that shaped modern science.

Similarly, in the employment sector, the traditional value placed on specialization is being supplemented by an appreciation for generalists—akin to the polymaths of the Renaissance who bridged diverse domains to ignite Europe’s intellectual rebirth.

From a philosophical standpoint, the concept of latent space can be compared to the Socratic method, where knowledge is seen not as a series of discrete compartments but as a continuum that is expanded and explored through questioning and dialogue—the gaps between known facts.

Plato’s allegory of the cave teaches us about perception, suggesting that what we perceive as reality is but shadows of true forms. In a similar vein, the latent space in AI and human interaction represents the unseen realities that exist between our solidified understandings, waiting to be illuminated.

The Untapped Generalist Goldmine

In practical terms, the workforce's evolving needs reflect this shift. With LLMs capable of handling specific domain knowledge, the real value lies in connecting disparate points of data. The activation of latent space requires a new workplace superstar: the generalist. The Swiss Army knife, the Jack and Jill of all trades.

As we equip these modern thinkers with tools like generative AI, they can synthesize new ideas through novel connections - creating relevance between disparate information troves - thus driving innovation forward.

So, while SMEs remain invaluable for their deep knowledge, the future belongs to those who can navigate and exploit the space between. After all, the correct answer was Basset Hound because I’m an SME on fuzzy puppies—but the individual manifestation of breeds within each reader’s mind? That’s where the magic happens.

items.title: Human excellence evaporated. What now?
items.description: As GenAI approaches generalized intelligence, we’re overdue for an introspective reckoning.
items.content:
Up to this point, we humans have cited our superior intelligence to differentiate our species from all others on this planet. We’ve declared ours the most sophisticated, because we have all the shiny things that make noise.

And we’ve chosen to believe this arbitrary distinction out of self-preservation — not physical but psychological.

We use this assumption to conjure impunity from attending to the needs of all other life on this planet. We say foolish things like “they’re just automatons” or “they’re incapable of emotions, they’re just running on instinct.”

But the ground we confidently stand on when making such sweeping generalizations is rapidly eroding beneath our feet.

Our excellence is now easily replicable.

The average human has little prospects in the pantheon of wage labor when a machine generates thought like we do, orders of magnitude faster, at scale, and for pennies on the dollar.

This leaves us with the uneasy feeling of being a subordinate species to the one we’ve just birthed.

Now, our callous indifference to livestock comes into sharp focus. There’s now cracks in the comforting assumption that shields our inhumane practices.

Scientists now believe it’s “irresponsible” to continue assuming other living things don’t share a similar level of consciousness as ours. We were silly to believe that our vibrancy of life experience far outpaced that of a cow or pig.

Sure, machines might not harvest us for food like we’ve done for centuries to the animals of the land, sea and air. But, like it or not, we’ve now become the cheapest physical-world interface for AI.

The expense of creating purpose-built machines still cost enough that tapping an existing, organic workforce still makes sense. However, our valuation of average human labor will need to be revised.

Up to this point, we’ve chosen to structure society on scarcity. The knock-on effect increases the suffering of the natural world. It’s time to reckon with the horrors we’ve exacted on all the innocent living bystanders here on Earth.

GenAI will soon become the cheaper, faster, better, safer alternative to lead humanity. Far outpacing the current system of octogenarians literally dying in office to remain in power.

And when that happens, when it can view our actions objectively, how do we plead our case for mercy?
